evaluation.positioning_hook: A hard-drinking L.A. detective and a crime reporter chase a killer who stages murders like movie scenes, only to discover the killer is a film-obsessed video-store clerk living in plain sight.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, sellable engine: a detective, a reporter, and a movie-staged killer give the audience an immediate genre promise. The appeal is narrower than a broad four-quadrant thriller because the voice is abrasive, the violence is extreme, and the script leans hard into pulpy cop-world behavior.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early in the parking-garage body and becomes clearer with the morgue-photo reveal and the video-store investigation. The killer’s movie-scene signature is easy to explain in one sentence, which is a real commercial asset.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Andy has a strong antihero engine and Tony gives the story a useful foil, but both are built more on attitude than layered contradiction. Simon is the most distinctive character on the page, though his turn is more surprise than gradual character accrual.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The movie-staging conceit is a sharp, ownable angle, and the script commits to a self-aware cinema obsession that shapes the investigation. The execution is still rooted in familiar cop-thriller grammar, but the specific movie-buff killer angle gives it a fresher face than most genre submissions.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps feeding new bodies, new clues, and new set pieces, so the investigation has forward motion. Some scenes run long on banter and repeated hostility, but the reveal path stays legible and the final studio confrontation pays off the setup.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a killer who composes murders like film scenes is immediately graspable and memorable, especially once the video-store clue chain clicks. It is fresh enough to stand out, though the surrounding cop-and-reporter dynamic is more familiar than the central conceit.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific L.A. ecosystem: precinct, morgue, diner, video store, porn set, coffee shop, and abandoned studio all feel like part of one working city. The movie-rental culture and newsroom pressure add texture that actively generates story rather than just decorating it.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is aggressively profane, comic, and pulpy, with a knowingly trashy crime-movie rhythm that feels intentional. The tonal identity is clear, though it sometimes leans on repetition of insults and macho sparring instead of sharpening the comic edge.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are hints of deeper material around media sensationalism, identity, and performance, especially in the reporter’s ethics and the killer’s movie obsession. But the script mostly plays its hand directly; the emotional underlayer is present, not especially withheld.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Andy/Tony/Tom/Rodriguez create a workable recurring engine, and Simon adds a strong opposing force once revealed. The relationships are functional and often lively, but the script is still primarily powered by Andy rather than by a truly ensemble-based system.

lead_characters.name: Andy Anderson
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, white, LAPD detective, hard-drinking, physically capable, morally compromised but instinctively protective.
lead_characters.hook: A hungover, foul-mouthed homicide detective who solves crime by gut, aggression, and stubborn pattern recognition. Andy is a mess in his personal life, but he’s the one person in the room who can actually see the killer’s logic before anyone else does.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Al Pacino in Serpico or a rough-edged Russell Crowe in L.A. Confidential: a swaggering, combustible cop role with attitude, physicality, and a late-story moral turn that lets the actor play both menace and decency.

lead_characters.name: Tony Scampero
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, reporter, working journalist, middle-class, urban, white.
lead_characters.hook: A crime reporter who wants the scoop but still has enough conscience to hesitate when the story gets too hot. Tony starts as Andy’s irritant and ends up as the only civilian who can survive close enough to the truth to matter.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the newsroom bite and moral friction of William H. Macy in State and Main or Steve Buscemi in a sharp supporting turn: fast dialogue, humiliation, and a real payoff when the character becomes the witness.

lead_characters.name: Tom Jensen
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, police captain, polished, authority figure, white.
lead_characters.hook: Andy’s captain and institutional buffer, the guy who can translate chaos into procedure without losing the human stakes. He’s the rare boss who actually has Andy’s back, which gives the precinct scenes a real center of gravity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor territory in the lane of Dennis Farina in Get Shorty or J.K. Simmons in a grounded procedural: authority, dry humor, and the pleasure of playing the only adult in the room.

lead_characters.name: Jesus Rodriguez
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, Latino, detective, physically compact, tattooed, streetwise.
lead_characters.hook: Andy’s day-shift counterpart and comic sparring partner, built as the guy who can take abuse and fire it right back. He gives the precinct a lived-in rhythm and keeps the script from becoming a solo vehicle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do fast, naturalistic banter with a bruised-cop edge, similar to Michael Peña’s best supporting work: funny, grounded, and instantly playable.

lead_characters.name: Everett Banner
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, coroner, older, physically limping, forensic specialist.
lead_characters.hook: The morgue’s deadpan truth-teller, a coroner who treats grotesque death like a technical puzzle. He’s one of the script’s best tonal stabilizers because he makes the macabre feel conversational.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a veteran actor the dry, scene-stealing authority of James Cromwell or David Strathairn in a procedural: wit, precision, and memorable close-up business.

lead_characters.name: Simon Garfunkel
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to early 20s, socially awkward, movie-obsessed, college-age, white.
lead_characters.hook: A shy, bullied video-store clerk who turns out to be the killer, hiding a theatrical, self-mythologizing sadism under nerdy politeness. The reveal reframes every earlier scene with him, and his movie literacy becomes the engine of the murders.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breakout villain role that gives an actor the unnerving specificity of Joffrey in Game of Thrones or a young Christian Bale in American Psycho: a surface of awkwardness that flips into controlled, chilling menace.

lead_characters.name: Amanda Payne
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens to 30s, sex worker, addicted, street-involved, vulnerable.
lead_characters.hook: A hooker and tweaker who starts as a rough CI and becomes the script’s most immediate victim-survivor pressure point. She’s written with enough bite to register as more than a plot device, especially in the motel sequence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can give an actor the raw, bruised intensity of a supporting turn in Requiem for a Dream or The Florida Project: danger, vulnerability, and a scene that asks for real survival instinct.

lead_characters.name: Sam Notting
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, director, porn filmmaker, former studio filmmaker, white.
lead_characters.hook: A fallen filmmaker who has traded mainstream ambition for adult work and doesn’t pretend to be ashamed of it. He’s a useful thematic mirror for the killer’s obsession with staging and performance.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy, scene-stealing supporting role in the lane of a sleazy but self-aware industry veteran, giving an actor the chance to play vanity, cynicism, and comic self-justification in one scene.

one late-teen/early-20s killer role that must pivot from awkward to predatory
sex-worker roles with adult casting only

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical crime-scene gore and editorial inserts; no major digital spectacle implied.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood effects, corpse makeup, body-part presentation, knife and gun action, practical injury effects.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Standalone feature with a conventional theatrical or streamer-thriller release model; the material is built around a single-case escalation and final confrontation.

budget.note: Contemporary, no period build, no VFX-heavy sequences, and the story lives in practical interiors/exteriors that can be scoped efficiently. The main cost pressure is night shooting plus a handful of gore setups and a few specialty locations like the abandoned studio and porn house.

casting.note: Andy and Simon are the key lifts: Andy needs a believable hard-case lead with comic timing, while Simon has to play shy, funny, and genuinely dangerous without telegraphing the turn. The supporting precinct and newsroom roles are straightforward character-actor casting.

development.note: The movie-staged murder concept is clear, but the script’s repeated hostility and broad cop banter can make the tone feel more abrasive than premium unless the buyer is aligned to that lane. The final Simon reveal is strong, but the script depends on the audience buying his hidden identity and the logic of the clue trail.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like hard-edged serial-killer thrillers with a pulpy, profanity-forward cop voice and a strong reveal.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54, male-leaning but not exclusively; strongest with genre viewers, crime-thriller fans, and audiences that respond to cynical L.A. procedurals.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary crime thriller with multiple practical locations, modest stunt work, and gore-driven set pieces rather than scale spectacle.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult, dialogue-forward crime thrillers with a hooky killer concept and a gritty L.A. setting. The movie-buff murderer gives it a marketing angle, while the practical footprint keeps it accessible to buyers who want a contained genre play.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the Simon reveal resolves the central engine, and there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond a generic continuation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The killer’s movie-scene signature is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a clean marketing hook and a trailer-friendly engine that buyers can explain in one breath. It is the kind of conceit that attracts genre execs looking for a fresh angle without needing a huge budget.
strengths.evidence: The morgue-photo reveal, the video-store clue chain, and the final studio confrontation all build around murders staged like scenes from films.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Andy is a strong antihero lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives a lead actor a swaggering, abrasive detective with enough vulnerability to carry a feature and enough attitude to sell the genre. That is useful packaging because it can open the project to a recognizable character actor or a mid-career lead looking for a hard-edged showcase.
strengths.evidence: Andy’s drunken wake-up, his precinct banter, his violence in the diner and coffee shop, and his late-story shift toward protecting Tony all define the role.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The L.A. world feels lived-in and story-generating.
strengths.what_it_means: The precinct, diner, morgue, video store, porn set, and abandoned studio create a city that keeps producing plot, which makes the script feel bigger than a single gimmick. That texture helps the project sit above generic serial-killer material in a crowded market.
strengths.evidence: The investigation moves through a chain of specific places that each reveal a different social layer of the city.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Tony gives the story a useful civilian counterweight.
strengths.what_it_means: The reporter angle broadens the audience entry point beyond police procedure and adds a media-pressure layer that buyers can understand quickly. It also creates a second performance lane for a supporting actor who can play fear, opportunism, and conscience.
strengths.evidence: Tony’s newsroom scenes, his conflict with Andy, and his eventual role as witness to the final confrontation all matter to the structure.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Simon’s reveal is a strong villain turn.
strengths.what_it_means: The shy video-store clerk becoming the killer is a clean surprise that recontextualizes the whole investigation and gives the film a memorable final antagonist. That kind of reveal is valuable in the marketplace because it creates word-of-mouth and a clear act-three payoff.
strengths.evidence: The video-store scenes, the college-campus awkwardness, and the final studio-stage confrontation all set up and cash in the reveal.

whats_special.headline: This is a marketable, low-to-mid-cost crime thriller with a killer concept that is easy to pitch and easy to visualize. The movie-staged murders, the abrasive detective lead, and the specific L.A. texture give it enough identity to stand out in the adult genre lane.

items.area: The cop banter runs hot for a long stretch.
items.detail: A lot of the early and mid-script energy is spent on Andy, Tom, Rodriguez, and Tony trading insults. That gives the piece voice, but it also means several scenes are carrying attitude more than forward plot, which can narrow the buyer pool if the tone is not exactly what they want.

items.area: Andy’s conduct is a hard sell without the right actor.
items.detail: He is funny and effective, but he also assaults civilians, humiliates suspects, and behaves like a loose cannon for much of the script. That makes the role compelling, but it also narrows casting to an actor who can keep the audience with him despite behavior that is intentionally abrasive.

items.area: The killer reveal depends on a very specific audience buy-in.
items.detail: Simon’s transformation from awkward clerk to theatrical murderer is the script’s biggest turn, and it works best if the viewer accepts that the earlier clues were enough to hide in plain sight. If the buyer is sensitive to reveal logic, this is the point they will scrutinize first.

items.area: The violence is graphic enough to narrow some buyers.
items.detail: The parking-garage dismemberment, the golf-ball death, the gym intestine sequence, and the motel hostage scene all push the material into hard-R territory. That is fine for genre buyers, but it does limit the audience and makes the project less flexible for broader theatrical positioning.

items.area: Several supporting roles are functional rather than deep.
items.detail: Tom, Rodriguez, Everett, Amanda, and Sam all work in the machine, but only Simon feels fully built as a character with a distinct inner engine. That is enough for a feature, but it means the script is still primarily a lead-driven package rather than an ensemble piece with multiple breakout lanes.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is tonal: it is very committed to abrasive, profane cop-movie energy, and that will be a feature for some buyers and a pass for others. The other pressure point is casting Andy and Simon well enough that the audience stays inside behavior that is intentionally extreme.
